Team Name: Frana Fam

Challenge Division: Elementary 
Title: Which amendment, when mixed 
with mars regolith, has the best growth for 
radishes and peas? 
Hypothesis: We think our peas will grow 
the best in the Mars regolith and 
vermicompost mixture. We think our 
radishes will grow the best in the Mars 
regolith and coconut coir amendment 
mixture. 
 
 
Independent Variables: The soil composition of our pots were 
deliberately varied to evaluate the best amendment to use with the Mars 
regolith. We tested four different amendments at a 50% to 50% ratio. We 
conducted this experiment on both peas and radishes. 
 
 
2 pots with 50% Mars Regolith + 50% Jiffy Seed Starter Mix 
 
1 pot with 100% Jiffy Seed Starter Mix 
 
2 pots with 50% Mars Regolith + 50% Promix Seed Starter 
 
1 pot with 100% Promix Seed Starter 
 
2 pots with 50% Mars Regolith + 50% Vermicompost with Worms 
 
1 pot with 100% Vermicompost with Worms 
 
2 pots with 50% Mars Regolith + 50% Burpee Coconut Coir 
 
1 pot with 100% Burpee Coconut Coir 
Dependent Variables: We measured the health of our plants based on 
their growth height and number of leaves and fruit produced. Every two 
days we measured the plants height. We noted when a fruit was produced 
and harvested. At the end of the experiment we counted the number of 
leaves on all of the remaining healthy plants. We recorded any additional 
notes as important information presented. 
Measurements: Every two days we measured the plants height from the 
base of the plant, at soil level, to the highest point of the plant. We noted 
when a flower was produced and when fruit harvested. At the end of the 
experiment we counted the number of leaves on all of the remaining 
healthy plants. At the end of the 8 weeks we removed the reddish plants to 
see if any radishes had grown. We recorded any additional notes as 
important information presented. 
Control: We worked to create the most controlled environment possible in 
our home in an effort to simulate the controlled environment of space. We 
Grow Set Up
Preparing the Soil
Green House for Plant Mars

set up an indoor greenhouse that helped us keep a constant temperature 
and humidity. We equipped the greenhouse with plant mat heaters to help 
control the soil temperature, we suspended lights that were on a timer so 
that the plants would have 12 hours of light each day, and we only 
removed the plants to record data and water them. We measured the soil’s 
moisture level every 2 days and water them till they were in the wet zone 
on the meter. 
Results for Peas: 
Our Pea plants started out very strong. They sprouted in 4 days and grew 
on average at 2 cm per day. Our controls grew taller but all of the plants 
were healthy. 
We hypothesized that our pea plants would grow best in the compost/
mars regolith. Our hypothesis failed as there was not clear evidence that 
they did better in one type of amendment over another. 
When our plants started wilting and drying we did a soil test and found 
that our soil for the non-control pots had no nitrogen and our controls had 
very little. We then decided to add nitrogen to the water to see if this 
would help save our plants. We were either too late or added too much 
because they completely died after this. 
Our plants did succeed in producing a total of 3 pea pods measuring 2 1/2 
cm each (1 pod from promix/mars, 1 pod from compost/mars, and 1 in 
the compost control). So we conclude that pea plants would be a good 
plant for further research on future plant mars research and as a possible 
food source for space farms. 
If we were to repeat this experiment, we would do a soil test before we 
plant the seeds to see if anything should be added before starting. Then 
we would regularly monitor the soil to see if the plants would need more 
nutrients as they grew and used what is in the soil. 
After the grow term was done we removed the pea plants from their pots 
and found that the roots in the control pots were much more elaborate; 
they were spread out and stretched to the bottom of the pot. The non-
control plants had fewer roots and they were located more at the surface 
of the pot. 
We are curious if the mars regolith settled to the bottom of the pots 
through the watering process. If we were to redo this experiment we 
would use clear pots so we could more easily observe the root structure 
and if the soil composition changed throughout the experiment.

Results For Radishes 
Our control radish plants sprouted and grew very quickly. No radish plants 
grew in our variable pots for the first 20 days. On Feb 22nd we replanted radish 
seeds in those pots and radish plants started growing in those pots quickly after. 
While all the plants grew, most of the variable pots did not live long. By March 
9th all but the compost/mars pots had died. We think that the plants were not 
getting the water they needed. After the experiment we removed the plants from 
their pots and found that the roots were all concentrated at the top of the pots 
and think when watered the water would seep down and out of the pots quickly, 
not providing the roots enough time to take in the water. 
We hypothesized that our radish plants would grow best in the coconut coir/
mars regolith. Our hypothesis failed as our radish plants grew best in the 
compost/mars mixture.

Measuring Radish Growth

All of the radishes plants grew long thin stems. If we were to do this experiment again we would move 
the light closer to the seedlings to help them not have to reach towards the light. 
The most interesting part of this experiment were the bonus plants that came up in our compost/mars 
mixture. On Feb 14th, an unidentified plant spouted in pot G1 and G2. This also happened in our pea 
plant tray. Because none of our radish plants were growing in the variable pots we decided to let these 2 
plants continue to grow and started tracking their data. Additional information on this can be found on 
the next page.

Results For Tomatoes 
Tomatoes were not a plant that we were 
planning on growing this year for Plant 
Mars. They were bonus or as our grandparents would call them, 
“volunteer” plants that came up for the compost we make from our 
kitchen scraps. 
After we decided to add the tomato plants to our experiment we hypothesized that they would not grow 
well. But we were excited to see what would happen. Our hypothesis was incorrect as both of these 
plants did very well. The variable plant with 50% compost & 50% mars regolith grew larger than our 
control, produced several flowers, and 1 small tomato has started. 
After removing the tomato plants from the soil we can see that the compost helped to gave the roots 
room to spread out and grow. The roots were able to move down into the mars regolith in a way that 
they didn’t for our other plants.
